cards.front: Short note: Milestones that shaped research ethics and GCP

points: US Federal Food and Drugs Act: against adulterated or misbranded food and drugs
Sulphanilamide elixir tragedy: untested solvent (an antifreeze) killed over 100 people
Nuremberg Code after Nazi camp experiments: informed consent, right to withdraw
Promoted for morning sickness; babies born without limbs or with severe deformities
Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association): ethical base of ICH-GCP
Belmont Report (US National Commission, under the National Research Act 1974)
CIOMS guidelines applying Helsinki to modern research
ICH-GCP finalised 1996, effective 1997

cards.front: What did the Nuremberg Code establish?
cards.back: Drawn up in 1947 after unethical experiments on prisoners in Nazi camps during World War II, it established that research subjects must give informed consent and must be free to withdraw from an experiment at any time.

cards.front: What is the Declaration of Helsinki and why does it matter for trials?
cards.back: A statement of ethical principles for medical research on human subjects, issued by the World Medical Association in 1964 and regularly updated. It sets the widely accepted ground rules for human research and forms the ethical base of ICH-GCP: trials must be conducted according to its principles.

cards.front: What do the CIOMS guidelines add to the Declaration of Helsinki?
cards.back: The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (guidelines first published 1993) gives detailed guidance on applying Helsinki to present-day research: HIV/AIDS research, post-study availability of treatment, women as subjects, confidentiality, compensation for adverse events and consent, while avoiding unnecessary suffering and weighing risk against benefit.

cards.front: Complete: the four principles of medical ethics (Beauchamp and Childress)
cards.text: {{Autonomy}}: the person's right to make choices and hold views; {{beneficence}}: do good and contribute to welfare; {{non-maleficence}}: do no intentional harm; {{justice}}: treat everyone equally and share benefits fairly.

cards.front: What are the cardinal principle and the principle of precaution in research on human participants?
cards.back: The cardinal principle is respect for the dignity of persons. Precaution and risk minimisation require care at every stage so that participants and affected communities face minimum risk and no known irreversible harm. All guidelines demand both ethical and scientific review and informed consent.

cards.front: How do ICH-GCP and WHO-GCP differ?
cards.back: ICH-GCP was designed to harmonise technical requirements for drug registration across the US, Japan and EU and has 13 principles. WHO-GCP was written as a teaching tool for countries without their own guideline and has 14 principles (its principles 5 and 6 are combined in ICH-GCP). Both aim to promote good clinical practice.

cards.front: Short note: The 13 principles of ICH-GCP

points: Conduct per Declaration of Helsinki and regulations
Benefits must justify foreseeable risks
Subjects' rights, safety and well-being outweigh science and society
Freely given informed consent
Confidentiality of records
Adequate non-clinical and clinical data on the product
Scientifically sound, clear, detailed protocol
Prior IRB/IEC approval and protocol compliance
Medical decisions by a qualified physician or dentist
Staff qualified by education, training and experience
Records allow accurate reporting and verification
Investigational product made and stored per GMP and used per protocol
Quality systems for every aspect of the trial

cards.front: What are the Indian GCP guidelines and what is the principle of essentiality?
cards.back: CDSCO set up an expert committee that produced India's first GCP document in 2001, modelled on WHO, US FDA, ICH and EU guidelines. It lists 10 ethical principles in line with Helsinki, including informed consent, community agreement, non-exploitation, privacy and confidentiality, risk minimisation, and accountability and transparency of investigators and sponsors. Essentiality means human subjects should be used only when absolutely necessary and no alternative exists. The NDCT Rules 2019 define "GCP guidelines" as the CDSCO guidelines adopted by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board.

cards.front: What role do the ICMR ethical guidelines play in Indian research?
cards.back: ICMR issued Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Subjects in 2000, with planned periodic revision to keep researchers updated on bioethics. Ethics committees for biomedical and health research (as opposed to drug trials) are constituted under ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants. Standard guidelines also make studies comparable across centres and help prevent duplicated research.

cards.front: Short note: Composition of an ethics committee for biomedical and health research (ICMR)

points: Chairperson or vice-chairperson: respected, experienced, not affiliated with the institution
Member secretary: staff of the institution with research and ethics experience
Basic medical scientist
Clinician(s)
Legal expert (law degree)
Social scientist, philosopher, ethicist or theologian (may be from an NGO)
Lay person from the community
At least 5 members, medical and non-medical, technical and non-technical
At least one non-affiliated member; preferably the lay person
No decision valid without quorum
GCP or human-protection training (within 6 months of appointment)
Declare conflicts of interest; sign confidentiality agreement
Name, profession and affiliation made public

cards.front: Complete: categories of ethics committee review by risk
cards.text: Proposals with less than minimal risk (e.g. research on educational practice) may be {{exempted}} from review; those with minimal risk (e.g. studies of already approved drugs or devices) get {{expedited}} review; those with more than minimal risk, or involving {{vulnerable}} groups such as children or psychiatric patients, need {{full}} committee review. The {{member secretary}} screens and categorises proposals.

cards.front: What kinds of ongoing review does an ethics committee carry out after approval?
cards.back: Periodic review of ongoing research at intervals of 6 months to 1 year; continuing review of any new information and adverse events; and interim review in special circumstances by a sub-committee, re-examined by the full committee as needed (e.g. quarterly).

cards.front: What decisions can an ethics committee reach, and how are records kept?
cards.back: Approval (only minor changes), approval with modifications, resubmission with more information, or outright disapproval. Decisions are preferably by consensus; invited subject experts give opinions but do not decide. Minutes are approved and signed by the chair, documents are confidential, and records are kept for 5 years after the trial ends.

cards.front: Short note: What an ethics committee reviews in a proposal

points: Protocol; participant information sheet and consent form with translations
Investigator's brochure; PI's CV
Insurance or compensation; investigator-sponsor agreement
Rationale and essentiality; specific objectives
Design, sample size, statistics; justification of controls
Withdrawal and termination criteria; monitoring; emergency facilities
Recruitment and inclusion/exclusion
Risk-benefit for individual and community
Medical care, compensation for research injury, confidentiality
Adequacy and clarity of information; contact persons
Justification for including those unable to consent
Conflicts of interest of investigator, institution and sponsor

cards.front: What is clinical equipoise and why does it matter ethically?
cards.back: Genuine uncertainty among experts about which treatment is better. It justifies randomising patients, because the trial is done precisely because doubt exists. Placebo-controlled trials are argued to violate equipoise and the principle of beneficence when a proven effective therapy is already available.

cards.front: What does the Declaration of Helsinki say about placebo controls?
cards.back: It discourages placebo controls when an alternative treatment is available, since patients randomised to placebo would in effect be denied treatment; every patient, including controls, should get the best proven methods and not suffer unnecessary pain. Where an available treatment prevents death or irreversible harm, a placebo control is generally inappropriate.

cards.front: Short note: When is a placebo-controlled trial ethically justified?

points: No proven or approved therapy exists
Existing therapy is of doubtful or modest, inconsistent efficacy with frequent adverse effects, and the new drug is not expected to be better
Patients fully informed, autonomy kept, close monitoring, rescue treatment available, GCP followed
Existing therapy is highly and consistently effective: use an equivalence or non-inferiority design
Existing therapy prevents death or irreversible morbidity
Add-on design so all receive standard care
Minimal placebo exposure; early-escape and withdrawal rules
Smaller placebo arm; DSMB interim review

cards.front: What must the consent form of a placebo-controlled trial tell participants?
cards.back: What "placebo" means, in lay language; that they may receive it; why a placebo is used and what alternatives exist; how long they may be on placebo and the likely discomfort; the harm of not receiving or delaying effective treatment and that the condition may worsen; and that they may withdraw at any time.

cards.front: When is it ethical to use a placebo in clinical practice?
cards.back: Only with the patient's welfare as the sole motive, to relieve suffering, when the condition has an unpredictable course, standard treatment fails or is not tolerated, or no effective therapy exists. It must never replace effective treatment, must be stopped if ineffective, and the doctor should answer honestly if asked about it; if it helps and nothing better exists, stopping it is unethical.

cards.front: What is a conflict of interest in research, and how should a reader handle it?
cards.back: A situation where personal factors (e.g. funding or financial gain) could influence professional judgement or responsibilities. Such conflicts are common; what matters is whether they were recognised and managed. When appraising a paper, check the declared funding source and any statement on how a conflict was handled. Ethics committee members must also declare conflicts.

cards.front: How does ICD-11 define burnout, and what are its three dimensions?
cards.back: A syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, marked by (1) exhaustion or energy depletion, (2) mental distance from the job, negativism or cynicism, and (3) reduced professional efficacy.

cards.front: Short note: Burnout in doctors: causes, consequences and prevention

points: Workload: long hours, night duty, administrative tasks, patient overload
Poor teamwork and relationships; lack of reward, autonomy and job security
Work-family conflict; lack of resources and development opportunities
More major medical errors and adverse patient incidents
Lower patient satisfaction; doctors leave practice
Depression and coronary risk linked to effort-reward imbalance
"Traffic-light" model: stop and recognise, pause and find causes, then start coping and treatment
Flexible schedules
Mindfulness-based stress reduction, meditation
System-level changes in addition to individual measures

cards.front: What is the pharmacologist's role in medical education?
cards.back: Teaching undergraduates (pharmacology is a second-year MBBS and BDS subject), postgraduates (including thesis guidance), and nursing and pharmacy students. Content includes rational drug use and essential drugs, drug classes, effects, toxicity, ADRs and interactions, telling real drug information from promotional claims, dose calculation by age, sex and health status, and correct routes. Pharmacologists also educate practising doctors on rational use, new drugs, ADR reporting, drug audit and generic prescribing.

cards.front: How are pharmacology competencies organised in India's competency-based undergraduate curriculum (CBME)?
cards.back: Each competency is a coded statement of what the student should be able to do, numbered with the prefix PH (e.g. PH1.2 evidence-based medicine and TDM, PH1.43 rational antimicrobial use and stewardship, PH1.55 national health programmes, PH1.64 drug development, trial phases and GCP). Katzung's Indian edition maps each PH competency to the chapter that covers it.
